cells.tense: You are carrying what has to be carried, and it has found its own pace.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're holding. Say why it's worth the weight, out loud, once, to no one in particular.
cells.core:
You carry what needs carrying, and you do it without grinding. Not because it got lighter — because your grip found the shape of it. What you hold, you hold on purpose, and that shows in how people bring you things.

There's a rhythm here you didn't have to force. You move at the speed the weight allows, and the weight moves at the speed you can bear. Not endurance as a grind — endurance as a pace you chose. When you imagine what this could feed next, it isn't more weight. It's a direction that grows from how you already stand.
cells.sheetLine: You hold what you hold deliberately, at a pace you chose.
cells.verb: moving at the speed the weight allows instead of pushing past it
cells.place: the place where you hold what can't be set down

cells.tense: You are bracing for a load that hasn't shown up, and the bracing is already costing you.
cells.ask: Pick one future worry. Do one concrete thing about it now, then put it down for the rest of the day.
cells.core:
You're steadying yourself under things that haven't been handed to you yet. The load-bearing starts before the weight arrives — you take the posture of what might come and plant your feet under it. That is real work and it doesn't show anywhere.

The strength you have is real. You're spending it early, on loads that may not arrive. In your head there's a version where you hold everything well, and you're living in that version instead of this one. Past a point, being ready stops being ready and becomes a rehearsal for a scene nobody's written. Most of what's on your back is the bracing itself.

cells.tense: You put something down before you knew whether it would hold, and you haven't gone back for it.
cells.ask: Go back to one thing you set down and stay with it for one hour, no measuring whether it's working.
cells.core:
You can carry, and you've stopped picking things up. Holding through one more stretch stopped being something you could see the point of, so you set it down and walked away. The strength didn't go anywhere. The picking back up did.

What's absent isn't strength. It's the willingness to take the weight back on, one piece at a time, knowing you'll have to wait for it to mean anything. That waiting is where you stand now, and it's hard to trust. Bearing things well doesn't get rewarded, and you've learned to hold back because of it. What you carried well once is still yours to carry.
cells.sheetLine: You have the strength. You've stopped picking things back up.
cells.verb: moving at the speed the weight allows instead of pushing past it

cells.tense: You are already bearing what the people around you lean on, and you talk about it like it's just how things are.
cells.ask: Tell one person one thing you've been holding for them, and say it plainly, as yours.
cells.core:
People lean on you and you don't count it. Someone rests, someone else doesn't fall, and you describe it as just the way things are. This is running in you, and nobody's claiming it.

It is steady and it doesn't ask for credit. That's part of why it works. But something in you has been treating what you carry as facts of the day instead of a choice you keep making. You didn't get handed this. You built it, one load at a time. Naming that isn't vanity. It's the difference between being strong and knowing you're strong, and the second one is what lets you decide what gets carried next.
cells.sheetLine: You carry it daily. You call it the way things are.
cells.verb: moving at the speed the weight allows instead of pushing past it
